cells.tense: You stand in the middle of what you've grown, and the season is doing its work.
cells.act: make the fair call about a feeling, yourself
cells.ask: When a feeling runs hot this week — yours or a moment's — settle it on your own terms: name it, weigh it, decide what it deserves. Skip the extra trip through somebody else's opinion.
cells.core:
Something ripe sits close at hand, and you know what it needs. You've been taking what's done and working it into ground for what comes next, and it shows: nothing forced, nothing rushed, time given and time returned. Whoever tends this alongside you can feel how much steadier the work goes because you already read the season correctly.

Keep one habit going. When something is running hot, you don't need anyone to rule on what's fair — that judgment lives with you. Take one feeling that's been lingering and settle it plainly, then set it down. The verdict is yours to reach without the extra pass through someone else's read on it.
cells.sheetLine: You know what's ripe and what to let fall.
cells.verb: turning what's finished into ground something new can grow in
cells.place: in the part of life that tends what's still growing

cells.tense: The next season is already mapped in your head, and you're planting for it before this one has finished.
cells.act: hold space for what someone feels without fixing it
cells.ask: Before you fix the next thing for someone, give what they feel five minutes of room — ask, listen, stay — and then decide if fixing is what they came for.
cells.core:
You're several steps past the calendar. Seedlings go in before the last frost has finished, beds get turned while things are still living in them. The caring is genuine and it's running faster than what it cares for can follow. Next year's harvest is already in your hands while this year's is still in the ground.

What's thin here isn't restraint. It's standing where something is alive and letting it be alive next to the person it belongs to. Pick a shared thing you'd usually rearrange, leave it as it is, and stay there with whoever it matters to. Ask what it's like for them and stay in the answer.
cells.sheetLine: You're planting next year's beds before this one's grown.

cells.tense: You turned the old into ground once, and the pen for this plot has been down a long while.
cells.act: feed the drive a little at a time
cells.ask: Choose a small tending that still matters to you and do five minutes of it today, then five again tomorrow. That much, and then stop — no catching up.
cells.core:
You were good at this once, taking what was done and working it into ground that would grow. Then something stopped, and the plot you used to keep hasn't been touched, and you still think of yourself as the one who keeps it. The hours that went into it go elsewhere now. That's the state of things — not laziness, not loss, just a chair nobody has sat down in.

What brings you back isn't a big push. It's a small act you actually want. Name the smallest tending you can think of — five minutes, once a day — and do that much. Feed the interest steadily instead of waiting for a large feeling to arrive. Whatever wants to grow next will show itself once the soil is being touched again.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped tending it a while back and stayed anyway.

cells.tense: You decide what gets released and what gets kept, and you call that the timing.
cells.act: set a boundary and hold it
cells.ask: Take a line you've been holding quietly — the thing you won't let near what you're growing — and make it concrete once: a locked gate, a deleted number, a returned key. Then keep it.
cells.core:
Something in what you keep has a keeper. What gets released, what stays, what the plot is allowed to become — those calls get made, and made by a steady hand that doesn't count itself as a hand. Ask about the choices and you'd say the plot simply works out that way, that the season decides. But the season has someone working it. That isn't a flaw, just an unsigned page.

Start with one edge. There's a line you've been holding, the one that keeps something harmful away from what you're growing, and it has a shape in the world: a boundary acted on, not announced. Make it concrete once — a gate shut, a name dropped from the list — and hold it. Then it's a line you know you're keeping, and the one keeping it is someone you can name.
cells.sheetLine: The gardener is you, and the garden says season.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is the Too Much core's 'the tomatoes go in before anyone asked' and 'people have stopped bringing you seedlings' — the record says over-control and pushing ahead of natural timing, but not that others withdraw; I've kept the picture inside one believable moment instead of generalizing about others' choices. A reader could reasonably object that their urgency isn't about growing things at all — the ask survives that, since the act (hold space for one person's feeling without fixing it) works whether the seat is a garden, a team, or a family, though 'seedlings' is doing more work than the record strictly gives. The writer's pet sentence in the draft was 'the future has a say in every decision' — it sounds like wisdom, but it describes a stance rather than a capacity, so the final Too Much core names the countdown instead of the philosophy.
